learningObjective: Understand what 'lowering' means across MLIR abstraction layers, and why lowering typically preserves semantics but changes the vocabulary used to express the computation.

canonicalClaims.claim: Progressive lowering in MLIR moves from higher-level (declarative, structural) dialects to lower-level (explicit buffers, loops, memory) dialects, preserving semantics while exposing more structure so that later optimizations and codegen can operate on it.
conditions: The lowering pipeline uses semantically valid conversions (bufferization respects tensor-level dataflow).
The end goal is executable code or a lower-level dialect.
nonImplications: Does not imply lowering by itself introduces or removes aliasing hazards.
Does not imply the lowered form is always the fastest form; later passes make that decision.

misconceptions.claim: Lowering raises the abstraction level so downstream layers can pattern-match on higher-level ops.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Lowering goes in the direction of more explicit / lower-level; raising is the opposite.

misconceptions.claim: The linalg-on-tensor and scf-on-memref forms are semantically inequivalent because aliasing rules differ.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Bufferization is defined to preserve semantics; it inserts copies or proves non-aliasing when required.

misconceptions.claim: Lowering emits Python source code at each step for user inspection.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Lowering is an internal IR-to-IR transformation, not source generation.

misconceptions.claim: Every compiler must go through exactly linalg -> scf -> memref -> llvm; alternative paths are invalid.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Many production pipelines skip stages or route to Triton/XLA/GPU dialects directly.

implementationFacts: MLIR bufferization converts linalg-on-tensor to linalg-on-memref
linalg tiling / vectorization typically runs after bufferization or on structured tensor form depending on pipeline
The final step is usually conversion to LLVM dialect and codegen
performanceScenarios: Exposing loop structure allows tiling and vectorization; each level unlocks a different transformation family.
